newsitem.title: HUNGARY: SOCCER-HUNGARY'S UJPEST PLANS SOCCER FLOTATION.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-HUNGARY'S UJPEST PLANS SOCCER FLOTATION.

text.p: Hungarian soccer club Ujpest plans to become the first club in Eastern Europe to go public, with a flotation on the Budapest Stock Exchange (BSE).
Club president, former Olympic fencing champion Bence Szabo, said he plans a radical overhaul of the club's structure in order to attract foreign investment.
"Football is no longer just a sport," Szabo told Reuters. "It has become part of the entertainment business."

Currently the soccer team is part of a larger sports club with 15 sections including water-polo and fencing. Szabo said he wants to create an independent football club, owned by a public limited company which will float on the BSE. Ujpest's 70-member executive will hold a general meeting on Monday to vote on separating out the football activities and debate the move to a new structure.

"Clubs don't live only from ticket receipts but from merchandising and a whole range of business activities. We need to change and my generation sees that Hungarian football has to be built on solid business foundations," said the 35-year-old Szabo, who won gold for Hungary in Barcelona in 1992.
"Going to the stock market would also allow small businessmen and supporters to have a stake in the club," he said, adding that the move could also attract much-needed foreign investment.
The club is currently in talks with French club Metz and Szabo said he hoped that others would show interest as Hungary lines up to become one of the first new members of the European Union.
Szabo would not be drawn on whether Ujpest would sell a majority share in the initial public offering.
The move is another sign of the increasingly important role private investors are taking in Hungarian football.
Two years ago, current champions MTK were bought by a Hungarian company Sportinvest, owned by Hungarian Gabor Varszegi, CEO of consumer goods retailer Fotex .
After winning promotion to the first division in 1995, MTK used Varszegi's cash to recruit many of Hungary's top players and this season won the league and cup double.
Brian Sturgess, of ING Barings in London, a media analyst who specialises in football stocks, said he welcomed Ujpest's plans.

"In Eastern Europe there is a move away from the communist-era model of the giant sports club financed by a ministry and there is a clear move towards private capital. This will accelerate, especially with the certain increase in the value of TV soccer rights in the region."
Sturgess said he believed an Ujpest flotation could be successful provided it attracts larger investors.
"Of course there will be local interest from small investors but to really succeed they need to attract institutional investors.
"The traditional emerging markets investor may stay away but I am sure that the communication funds and leisure funds would be interested."
Ujpest, known as Ujpest Dozsa during the communist era, when they were backed by Hungary's Interior Ministry, are one of Hungary's most successful clubs.

They have won the Hungarian championship 19 times and in 1969 reached the final of Europe's Inter-Cities Fairs Cup - the forerunner of the UEFA Cup. But following the change of system in 1989 the club struggled and in 1993 had to win a play-off in order to stay in the first division.
Last season, however, they finished second in the league earning a place in the UEFA Cup.
